kurals.tamil:
நன்மையும் தீமையும் நாடி நலம்புரிந்த
தன்மையான் ஆளப் படும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Nanmaiyum theemaiyum naadi nalampurindha
Thanmaiyaan aalap padum.
kurals.meaning: The person to be employed is the one who, after weighing both the good and the harm in a matter, is by nature drawn to do what is good.
kurals.elementary: Imagine picking a team captain. You don’t pick the kid who just does whatever pops into their head. You pick the one who stops, thinks “what could go right, what could go wrong?”, and then chooses the good way. That’s the kind of person you give a job to.
kurals.university: The chapter opens by naming the first qualification of a worthy agent: not raw talent but a settled disposition (தன்மை) that examines (நாடி) both benefit and harm and then inclines (புரிந்த) toward the good. Varadarasan and Kalaignar read it as a test of the candidate’s character, while Solomon Pappaiah reads it as an instruction to the appointee himself — once entrusted with a task, weigh its good and ill and do only what is good. Both readings converge on judgment joined to moral preference: discernment without a love of the good produces a clever but dangerous servant, and good intentions without discernment produce a well-meaning bungler. The pairing anticipates Aristotle’s prohairesis (deliberate choice) and the Upanishadic distinction between the good (śreyas) and the merely pleasant (preyas).

hinduism.quote_or_event: “The good and the pleasant approach man: the wise goes round about them and distinguishes them. Yea, the wise prefers the good to the pleasant, but the fool chooses the pleasant through greed and avarice.”
hinduism.explanation: Yama tells Nachiketas that both options present themselves to everyone; the wise person walks around them, examines them, and deliberately picks the good.
hinduism.tie_back: Exactly the Kural’s two-step: examine both sides (நாடி), then prefer the good (நலம்புரிந்த).
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong structural match on examining then choosing the good; the Upanishad’s context is spiritual liberation rather than employment.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Prove all things; hold fast that which is good.”
christianity.explanation: Paul tells the Thessalonians to test everything rather than accept it blindly, and then cling to whatever proves good.
christianity.tie_back: Testing plus holding to the good is the disposition the Kural says marks the employable person.
christianity._accuracy_note: Clear parallel of examine-then-choose-good; Paul addresses believers generally, not the selection of agents.

islam.quote_or_event: “Who listen to speech and follow the best of it. Those are the ones Allah has guided, and those are people of understanding.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an praises those who hear all that is said, weigh it, and follow the best part of it.
islam.tie_back: Hearing everything and following the best mirrors weighing good and ill and choosing the good.
islam._accuracy_note: Good match on discerning choice; not about appointment to office.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Give Thy servant therefore an understanding heart to judge Thy people, that I may discern between good and evil; for who is able to judge this Thy great people?”
judaism.explanation: Young King Solomon asks God not for wealth or long life but for the ability to tell good from evil so he can govern well.
judaism.tie_back: Solomon names the very faculty the Kural treats as the first qualification for anyone who governs or serves the state.
judaism._accuracy_note: Direct match on discerning good and evil for public service; Solomon is a ruler, not an employee.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Not by passing arbitrary judgments does a man become just; a wise man is he who investigates both right and wrong.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha says a person is truly just and wise only when they carefully investigate both sides before deciding.
buddhism.tie_back: Investigating both right and wrong is the Kural’s நன்மையும் தீமையும் நாடி.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Near verbal parallel; the verse concerns judges, which suits the Kural’s context of public officers.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: The Choice of Heracles: at a crossroads the young Heracles is approached by two women, Vice offering an easy, pleasant road and Virtue offering a hard but noble one; after hearing both, he chooses Virtue.
greek_mythology.explanation: Heracles listens to both sides before choosing, and the choice shapes the labours he later carries out for others.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The hero who weighs both paths and chooses the good is the one fit for great tasks, just as the Kural says.
greek_mythology.source: Prodicus’ fable as retold in Xenophon, Memorabilia 2.1.21-34
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Strong on weighing and choosing the good; the fable is about personal character rather than being chosen for work.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “...discern between good and evil, and so to choose always and everywhere the better life as he has opportunity.”
philosophy.explanation: At the end of the Republic, Socrates says the most important learning is the ability to tell good from evil and so always pick the better course.
philosophy.tie_back: Plato treats this power of discernment as the key qualification, just as the Kural makes it the first test of a worker.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Close on discernment plus preference for the better; set in the Myth of Er about choosing lives, not jobs.

kurals.tamil:
வாரி பெருக்கி வளம்படுத்து உற்றவை
ஆராய்வான் செய்க வினை.
kurals.transliteration:
Vaari perukki valampaduththu utravai
Aaraaivaan seyga vinai.
kurals.meaning: Let the work be done by the one who can widen the sources of income, turn them into growing prosperity, and look into and remove the troubles that arise along the way.
kurals.elementary: Think of someone looking after a lemonade stand. A good manager finds more customers, makes the stand earn more, and spots problems early, like running out of cups, and fixes them. That’s the person who should run the stand.
kurals.university: Kural 512 defines administrative competence in three verbs: பெருக்கி (expand the வாரி, the channels of revenue), வளம்படுத்து (turn income into lasting prosperity), and உற்றவை ஆராய் (look into whatever befalls, i.e., foresee and remove obstacles). Parimelazhagar and the modern commentators (Varadarasan, Pappaiah, Kalaignar) all read உற்றவை as the hindrances that threaten wealth, so the ideal agent is productive and protective at once. The couplet is strikingly economic: Valluvar judges the officer by measurable growth, not by birth or favour. Kautilya’s Arthashastra sets out the same standard, promoting superintendents who raise revenue and keeping in permanent service those who increase it loyally.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Those who increase the king’s revenue instead of eating it up, and are loyally devoted to him, shall be made permanent in service.”
hinduism.explanation: Kautilya’s manual of statecraft says officials who grow the treasury, rather than skimming it, should be kept on for good.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s ideal worker is the one who widens revenue and builds prosperity; Kautilya says that is exactly who should keep the job.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match in the same genre of statecraft literature.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Then came the first, saying, Lord, thy pound hath gained ten pounds. And he said unto him, Well, thou good servant: because thou hast been faithful in a very little, have thou authority over ten cities.”
christianity.explanation: In the parable of the pounds, the servant who multiplied his master’s money is rewarded with authority over ten cities.
christianity.tie_back: The one who increases what he is given is the one trusted with bigger work, which is the Kural’s criterion.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong match on growth as the qualification for charge; the parable is also an allegory of spiritual stewardship.

islam.quote_or_event: “[Joseph] said, “Appoint me over the storehouses of the land. Indeed, I will be a knowing guardian.””
islam.explanation: Joseph asks the king of Egypt to put him in charge of the nation’s grain stores, pointing to his knowledge and his ability to guard them.
islam.tie_back: Joseph both builds up reserves and guards against the coming famine, the growth-plus-foresight the Kural asks for.
islam._accuracy_note: Strong match on resource management and anticipating trouble; Joseph proposes himself here rather than being examined.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And it came to pass from the time that he appointed him overseer in his house, and over all that he had, that the LORD blessed the Egyptian’s house for Joseph’s sake; and the blessing of the LORD was upon all that he had, in the house and in the field.”
judaism.explanation: Once Potiphar makes Joseph overseer, his whole household and fields prosper.
judaism.tie_back: The right overseer makes the estate flourish, just as the Kural’s worker makes prosperity grow.
judaism._accuracy_note: Good on prosperity under a capable steward; the text credits divine blessing rather than Joseph’s technique.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Kutadanta Sutta, a wise chaplain advises a king troubled by banditry not to punish harder but to give seed and fodder to farmers, capital to traders, and proper wages to officials; the land then grows prosperous and peaceful.
buddhism.explanation: Growing the country’s sources of income removes the causes of disorder and fills the treasury.
buddhism.tie_back: Widening sources of income and removing what threatens prosperity is exactly the skill Kural 512 wants in an administrator.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Strong on economic policy; it describes an adviser’s policy rather than how to choose an officer.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: While Odysseus is away, his loyal swineherd Eumaeus builds pens and carefully tends and guards his master’s herds, keeping the estate going through twenty years of absence.
greek_mythology.explanation: Eumaeus is the model servant: he looks after and builds up his master’s wealth and guards it against the suitors’ waste.
greek_mythology.tie_back: He grows and protects what he has been given, like the Kural’s ideal worker, though on a small household scale.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Loose match: faithful stewardship rather than expanding revenue sources.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle retells how Thales, mocked for his poverty, foresaw a great olive harvest, rented all the olive presses in advance and made a fortune, and adds that statesmen should know such methods because states often need money.
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle treats knowing how to create wealth as a real part of statesmanship.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural likewise treats the ability to open new sources of revenue as a key qualification for public work.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Partial match on revenue-raising as a political skill; not about selecting agents.

kurals.tamil:
அன்பறிவு தேற்றம் அவாவின்மை இந்நான்கும்
நன்குடையான் கட்டே தெளிவு.
kurals.transliteration:
Anbarivu thetram avaavinmai innaankum
Nangudaiyaan katte thelivu.
kurals.meaning: Trust may safely be placed in the one who fully has these four: loyal love, knowledge, clear and firm judgment, and freedom from greed.
kurals.elementary: If you’re choosing someone to hold the class piggy bank, you want four things: they care about the class, they’re smart, they make clear decisions, and they don’t want the money for themselves. A person with all four is safe to trust.
kurals.university: Kural 513 is a compact job specification: அன்பு (attachment or loyalty to the ruler and the enterprise), அறிவு (knowledge), தேற்றம் (clarity and decisiveness; Varadarasan glosses it as the power to decide without doubt, Kalaignar as capacity to act), and அவாவின்மை (freedom from covetousness). நன்குடையான் stresses that the four must be held fully and steadily, not occasionally. Freedom from greed comes last, as the safeguard that keeps loyalty, knowledge and decisiveness from being turned to private gain. Jethro’s advice to Moses in Exodus 18:21, choosing capable men of truth who hate unjust gain, is an almost exact counterpart.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “One who is not envious but who is a kind friend to all living entities, who does not think himself a proprietor, who is free from false ego and equal both in happiness and distress, who is always satisfied and engaged in devotional service with determination and whose mind and intelligence are in agreement with Me—he is very dear to Me.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna describes the ideal devotee as friendly and kind, not possessive, content, and firm in determination.
hinduism.tie_back: Kindness (அன்பு), steady intelligence (அறிவு), firm determination (தேற்றம்) and contentment without possessiveness (அவாவின்மை) map closely onto the Kural’s four qualities.
hinduism._accuracy_note: The qualities line up well, but the Gita describes a beloved devotee, not a trusted officer.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Not given to wine, no striker, not greedy of filthy lucre; but patient, not a brawler, not covetous;”
christianity.explanation: Paul lists what a church overseer must be, stressing again and again that he must not love money.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, the New Testament makes freedom from greed a condition for being trusted with responsibility.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong on non-covetousness as a qualification; covers only part of the Kural’s four qualities.

islam.quote_or_event: “One of the women said, “O my father, hire him. Indeed, the best one you can hire is the strong and the trustworthy.””
islam.explanation: One of the daughters of the man of Midian recommends hiring Moses because he has shown both strength and trustworthiness.
islam.tie_back: Capability plus trustworthiness is the Qur’an’s short list; the Kural makes the same point with four qualities.
islam._accuracy_note: Classic Islamic proof text on hiring by merit; two criteria rather than four.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Moreover thou shalt provide out of all the people able men, such as fear God, men of truth, hating unjust gain; and place such over them, to be rulers of thousands, rulers of hundreds, rulers of fifties, and rulers of tens.”
judaism.explanation: Jethro tells Moses to pick capable, God-fearing, honest men who hate unjust gain, and put them in charge.
judaism.tie_back: Capability, integrity and hatred of gain closely match the Kural’s knowledge, clarity and freedom from greed.
judaism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match in both setting (appointing officials) and criteria.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha names three roots of wholesome action: non-greed (alobha), non-hatred (adosa, shown as goodwill) and non-delusion (amoha, i.e. wisdom).
buddhism.explanation: Good action grows from being free of greed, full of goodwill, and clear-seeing.
buddhism.tie_back: Goodwill, wisdom and non-greed correspond to three of the Kural’s four qualities (அன்பு, அறிவு, அவாவின்மை).
buddhism._accuracy_note: Conceptual overlap on three of four qualities; an ethical analysis, not a hiring rule.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Before sailing to Troy, Odysseus entrusts his whole household to his old friend Mentor, whose loyalty and good sense make him fit to keep it safe.
greek_mythology.explanation: Odysseus picks a friend known for loyalty and judgment to look after everything he owns.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Trust is given to someone with loyal love and wisdom, as the Kural recommends.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Illustrative only; Homer does not list Mentor’s qualities the way the Kural does.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “And to this end they ought to be wise and efficient, and to have a special care of the State?”
philosophy.explanation: Socrates says the city’s guardians must be wise and capable and must truly care for the city; later he denies them private property so greed cannot corrupt them.
philosophy.tie_back: Wisdom, capability, love of the city and freedom from acquisitiveness are almost exactly the Kural’s four qualities.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Very close match; the no-property safeguard comes from 416d-417b, not the quoted line.

kurals.tamil:
எனைவகையான் தேறியக் கண்ணும் வினைவகையான்
வேறாகும் மாந்தர் பலர்.
kurals.transliteration:
Enaivagaiyaan theriyak kannum vinaivagaiyaan
Veraagum maandhar palar.
kurals.meaning: Even after they have been tested and approved in every possible way, many people turn out differently once they are actually doing the work.
kurals.elementary: Someone can do great in a practice game and then play very differently in the real match. Tests help, but you only really know a person once they’re doing the actual job.
kurals.university: Having spent chapter 51 on testing (தெரிந்து தெளிதல்), Valluvar now admits its limits: however thoroughly a man is examined (எனைவகையான் தேறிய), the nature of the work itself (வினைவகையான்) can change him. Parimelazhagar sees here the corrupting pressure of office, wealth and power, and Pappaiah reads it as simple underperformance against expectations. The practical lesson, developed in Kural 520, is that selection must be followed by continuing supervision. The saying of Bias preserved by Aristotle, “rule will show the man,” states the same insight: power reveals what screening could not.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Just as it is impossible not to taste the honey or the poison that finds itself at the tip of the tongue, so it is impossible for a government servant not to eat up, at least, a bit of the king’s revenue.”
hinduism.explanation: Kautilya warns that officials in charge of revenue are constantly tempted, and even tested men may start to skim once the money is in their hands.
hinduism.tie_back: The work itself changes the worker, which is exactly the Kural’s warning.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong match on office corrupting tested men; Kautilya is more cynical than Valluvar.

christianity.quote_or_event: “This he said, not that he cared for the poor; but because he was a thief, and had the bag, and bare what was put therein.”
christianity.explanation: Judas, one of the Twelve chosen by Jesus himself, was trusted with the common purse and stole from it.
christianity.tie_back: Even someone chosen after close personal contact changed once he held the money, as the Kural warns.
christianity._accuracy_note: Vivid example; the Gospel frames it as a moral failing, not a lesson on how to manage staff.

islam.quote_or_event: “And recite to them, [O Muhammad], the news of him to whom we gave [knowledge of] Our signs, but he detached himself from them; so Satan pursued him, and he became of the deviators.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an tells of a man given great knowledge who later turned away and went astray.
islam.tie_back: Being gifted and approved at the start does not guarantee faithfulness later.
islam._accuracy_note: Next-best match: about spiritual backsliding rather than failing at an assigned task.

judaism.quote_or_event: “It repenteth Me that I have set up Saul to be king; for he is turned back from following Me, and hath not performed My commandments.”
judaism.explanation: Saul, chosen and anointed as king, failed once in power to carry out what he was charged with.
judaism.tie_back: Even a man chosen by the highest authority can turn out differently once in the role.
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong narrative parallel: chosen, installed, then changed in office.

buddhism.quote_or_event: Devadatta, a monk who had gained psychic powers, was ruined by the gain, honour and fame that came to him; the Buddha likens this to a plantain that dies after it bears fruit.
buddhism.explanation: Success and position changed Devadatta until he turned against the Buddha.
buddhism.tie_back: The pressures of a role can transform someone who once seemed sound, as Kural 514 observes.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Good match on corruption by position; monastic context.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Pindar tells how Tantalus, honoured by the gods and admitted to their table, could not bear his great good fortune and stole nectar and ambrosia to give to mortal companions, and was punished for ever.
greek_mythology.explanation: A man who seemed worthy of the gods’ trust betrayed it once he had it.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Trust granted after approval can still be abused, which is the Kural’s point.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Parallel on trust betrayed; nothing about testing for a task.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “This is why the saying of Bias is thought to be true, that ‘rule will show the man’; for a ruler is necessarily in relation to other men and a member of a society.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle quotes the sage Bias: you only discover what a person is really like when he holds power over others.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural says the same: many who passed every test turn out differently once they are actually in the job.

kurals.tamil:
அறிந்தாற்றிச் செய்கிற்பாற்கு அல்லால் வினைதான்
சிறந்தானென்று ஏவற்பாற் றன்று.
kurals.transliteration:
Arindhaatrich cheygirpaarku allaal vinaidhaan
Sirandhaanendru evarpaat randru.
kurals.meaning: A task should be given only to someone who knows how to do it and can push through the difficulties to finish it, never to someone just because he is a favourite or is held in high regard.
kurals.elementary: If the school play needs someone to run the lights, you don’t pick your best friend just because you like them. You pick the kid who knows how the lights work and won’t give up when something goes wrong.
kurals.university: The couplet sets competence against favouritism. Its first line gives the positive standard: அறிந்து (knowing the method), ஆற்றி (enduring obstacles) and செய்கிற்பான் (able to carry the task through). Its second line rules out appointing someone because he is சிறந்தான், someone the ruler holds dear or considers excellent in a general way. Pope’s “specious fav’rite” and Pappaiah’s gloss “thinking him one of our own (party, clan)” bring out the anti-nepotism edge. Plato’s ship of state, where sailors who have never learned navigation clamour to steer, dramatises the same danger.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Mahabharata, the blind king Dhritarashtra keeps backing his son Duryodhana out of fatherly attachment, although wiser advisers such as Vidura warn him that Duryodhana is unfit, and the result is the destruction of the Kuru line.
hinduism.explanation: Power is handed to someone because he is beloved, not because he is capable, and it ends in disaster.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural forbids exactly this: giving work to someone because he is dear rather than because he can do it.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Clear illustration of favouritism over fitness; a broad narrative, not a precept.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Ye know not what ye ask. Are ye able to drink of the cup that I shall drink of...?” ... “but to sit on my right hand, and on my left, is not mine to give, but it shall be given to them for whom it is prepared of my Father.”
christianity.explanation: When the mother of James and John asks for places of honour for her sons, Jesus replies that such positions depend on being able to bear the cost, not on a personal request.
christianity.tie_back: Positions go to those prepared and able, not to those with the right connections.
christianity._accuracy_note: Partial match; the setting is eschatological honour, not practical work.

islam.quote_or_event: “Abu Dharr, thou art weak and authority is a trust. and on the Day of judgment it is a cause of humiliation and repentance except for one who fulfils its obligations and (properly) discharges the duties attendant thereon.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet, though fond of his close companion Abu Dharr, declines to appoint him to office because he is not suited to its burdens.
islam.tie_back: Affection does not justify an appointment; only the ability to carry the duty does. This is the Kural exactly.
islam._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one: a beloved person is refused office for lack of the needed capacity.

judaism.quote_or_event: “But he forsook the counsel of the old men which they had given him, and took counsel with the young men that were grown up with him, that stood before him.”
judaism.explanation: King Rehoboam ignores experienced advisers and relies on his childhood friends, and the kingdom splits in two.
judaism.tie_back: Relying on familiar favourites instead of proven competence is the error the Kural warns against.
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong illustration; concerns counsellors rather than executors of tasks.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha says that one fit to go on a mission (duteyya) listens, gets others to listen, learns, remembers, understands, helps others understand, knows what is relevant and what is not, and does not stir up quarrels, and names Sariputta as having these qualities.
buddhism.explanation: Envoys are chosen by a list of specific skills.
buddhism.tie_back: Choosing an agent by demonstrated ability, not by rank, matches the Kural’s positive standard.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Good on skill-based selection; does not address favouritism directly.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Helios, bound by an oath and moved by love for his son, lets the inexperienced Phaethon drive the chariot of the sun; Phaethon loses control, scorches the earth, and Zeus strikes him down.
greek_mythology.explanation: A father gives a job to his son out of affection, although the son lacks the skill and strength for it.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the Kural’s warning come to life: give the task to one who can do it, not to one you love.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Very strong illustration; the oath adds a complication, but affection drives the grant.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “The sailors are quarrelling with one another about the steering—every one is of opinion that he has a right to steer, though he has never learned the art of navigation and cannot tell who taught him or when he learned...”
philosophy.explanation: Plato’s ship of state shows people who lack the skill fighting for the helm while the real navigator is ignored.
philosophy.tie_back: Plato and Valluvar agree that the helm belongs to whoever knows the craft, not to the popular or the favoured.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Strong match on competence over claims to office.

kurals.tamil:
செய்வானை நாடி வினைநாடிக் காலத்தோடு
எய்த உணர்ந்து செயல்.
kurals.transliteration:
Seyvaanai naadi vinainaadik kaalaththodu
Eydha unarndhu seyal.
kurals.meaning: First size up the person who will do the work, then size up the work itself, and then act once you are sure both fit the right time.
kurals.elementary: To bake a cake you need the right baker, the right recipe, and the right moment, so it’s ready when the party starts. Get all three right and it works.
kurals.university: Kural 516 sets out a three-part planning method: examine the doer (செய்வானை நாடி), examine the deed (வினைநாடி), and fit both to the proper time (காலத்தோடு எய்த உணர்ந்து). Pappaiah reads it as bringing agent and task together and then matching the pair to the moment. The couplet also draws on the earlier chapters on strength (48), time (49) and place (50). Plato’s specialisation principle, that things go best when each person does the one thing natural to him and does it at the right time, runs remarkably parallel.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “That gift which is given out of duty, at the proper time and place, to a worthy person, and without expectation of return, is considered to be charity in the mode of goodness.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna says a good action needs the right recipient, the right time and the right place.
hinduism.tie_back: The Gita’s check of person, time and place mirrors the Kural’s check of doer, deed and time.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Same triadic structure, applied to charity rather than delegation.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For which of you, intending to build a tower, sitteth not down first, and counteth the cost, whether he have sufficient to finish it?”
christianity.explanation: Jesus says a sensible builder works out beforehand whether he has what it takes to finish the job.
christianity.tie_back: Assess the task and your means before you start, as the Kural advises.
christianity._accuracy_note: Matches the planning step; says nothing about timing or choosing an agent.

islam.quote_or_event: “...and consult them in the matter. And when you have decided, then rely upon Allah.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet is told to consult his people, reach a considered decision, and then act with trust in God.
islam.tie_back: Deliberate first, then act decisively, is the procedure the Kural lays out.
islam._accuracy_note: Weak, next-best match: about deliberation in general, not assessing agent and timing.

judaism.quote_or_event: “To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven:”
judaism.explanation: Ecclesiastes teaches that every action has its proper time.
judaism.tie_back: This matches the Kural’s third element, fitting the work to the right moment.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “...a sense of himself, a sense of moderation, a sense of time, a sense of social gatherings, & a sense of distinctions among individuals.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha lists the qualities of a worthy person, among them knowing oneself, knowing the right time, and knowing how individuals differ.
buddhism.tie_back: A sense of time plus a sense of differences between people covers the Kural’s timing and choice of person.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Good overlap on time and persons; describes a monk’s qualities rather than a delegation procedure.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Kairos, the Greeks’ personification of the opportune moment, was shown in Lysippus’ statue with a lock of hair in front and bald behind: the moment can be seized as it comes but not once it has passed.
greek_mythology.explanation: The right moment has to be recognised and grasped before it slips away.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This reflects the Kural’s demand to fit the work to the proper time.
greek_mythology.source: Posidippus, epigram on Lysippus’ Kairos (Greek Anthology 16.275)

philosophy.quote_or_event: “...we must infer that all things are produced more plentifully and easily and of a better quality when one man does one thing which is natural to him and does it at the right time, and leaves other things.”
philosophy.explanation: Socrates argues that work goes best when each person does the task suited to his nature, at the right moment.
philosophy.tie_back: The right person, the right task and the right time is almost exactly the Kural’s formula.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match on doer, deed and time.

kurals.tamil:
இதனை இதனால் இவன்முடிக்கும் என்றாய்ந்து
அதனை அவன்கண் விடல்.
kurals.transliteration:
Idhanai idhanaal ivanmudikkum endraaindhu
Adhanai avankan vidal.
kurals.meaning: Once you have worked out that “this person will get this job done by these means,” hand the job over to him and leave it with him.
kurals.elementary: When your teacher knows you’re good at drawing and have the markers you need, she gives you the class poster to make and then lets you do it, without hovering over every line.
kurals.university: The couplet is built on demonstratives: இதனை (this task), இதனால் (by these means), இவன் (this man), and then அதனை அவன்கண் விடல் (leave that with him). Delegation follows a specific three-way match of task, resources and person; Varadarasan glosses இதனால் as “by this instrument” and Pappaiah as the manpower and money available. விடல் (to release) implies real handing over, not a nominal assignment followed by micromanagement. Jethro’s advice in Exodus 18, and the master in the parable of the talents who gives each servant a share “according to his several ability” and then departs, express the same trust.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Ramayana, when the monkey search parties set out for Sita, Rama gives his signet ring to Hanuman alone, judging that he is the one most likely to find her; Hanuman goes on to leap the ocean to Lanka and succeed.
hinduism.explanation: Rama works out who can accomplish the mission and with what, then entrusts it to him completely.
hinduism.tie_back: This man, this task, these means, then leave it to him: exactly the Kural’s formula.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And unto one he gave five talents, to another two, and to another one; to every man according to his several ability; and straightway took his journey.”
christianity.explanation: The master gives each servant as much as that servant can handle, then leaves them to get on with it.
christianity.tie_back: Allotting by ability and then really leaving is the heart of Kural 517.
christianity._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match on ability-based allocation and real delegation.

islam.quote_or_event: “Indeed, Allah commands you to render trusts to whom they are due and when you judge between people to judge with justice.”
islam.explanation: Classical exegesis applies this verse to giving offices and responsibilities to those who are rightly suited to them.
islam.tie_back: Giving each trust to the person it properly belongs to is the Kural’s entrusting principle.
islam._accuracy_note: Widely applied to appointments; the verse itself speaks of trusts in general.

judaism.quote_or_event: “...every great matter they shall bring unto thee, but every small matter they shall judge themselves; so shall they make it easier for thee and bear the burden with thee.”
judaism.explanation: Jethro tells Moses to let the appointed judges settle ordinary cases themselves and bring him only the hard ones.
judaism.tie_back: Real delegation to proven people, releasing the task to them, is what the Kural commands.
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong match on handing work over to capable agents.

buddhism.quote_or_event: When Devadatta leads a group of new monks away to Gayasisa, the Buddha sends Sariputta and Moggallana, his two ablest disciples, to win them back; they succeed.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha matches a delicate mission to the two disciples best suited to it and leaves it to them.
buddhism.tie_back: Choosing the right people for a specific task and trusting them to finish it reflects Kural 517.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Asked to pick a partner for a dangerous night raid on the Trojan camp, Diomedes chooses Odysseus for his cleverness and courage, saying that with him they could return even through blazing fire.
greek_mythology.explanation: Diomedes chooses the partner whose skills fit the mission.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Matching a particular person to a particular task by known ability echoes the Kural’s “this man will do this.”
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Good on selecting by capability; a peer choosing a partner rather than a ruler delegating.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle notes that masters who can afford it appoint a steward to run the household so that they themselves can devote their time to politics or philosophy.
philosophy.explanation: Once a competent manager is in place, the master hands over management entirely.
philosophy.tie_back: Handing work to a capable agent and leaving it with him is the Kural’s advice.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Partial match on delegation to a steward; slavery context.

kurals.tamil:
வினைக்குரிமை நாடிய பின்றை அவனை
அதற்குரிய னாகச் செயல்.
kurals.transliteration:
Vinaikkurimai naadiya pindrai avanai
Adharkuriya naagach cheyal.
kurals.meaning: After you have found out which work a person is suited to, make him fully responsible for that work, with the authority that goes with it.
kurals.elementary: If you find out your friend is the best goalkeeper, you don’t just let them try out. You make them the goalkeeper for real, with the gloves and everything.
kurals.university: The key word is உரிமை, suitability and also rightful ownership. Once fitness for a task (வினைக்குரிமை) has been established, the ruler must make the person its rightful holder (அதற்குரியனாக). Pappaiah stresses the second half: having appointed a man, let him exercise the powers of the post himself. The couplet thus balances Kural 517: 517 is about handing over, 518 about conferring the standing and authority that make the handover real. It is Valluvar’s closest statement of the specialisation principle, which Plato made the definition of justice and the Gita discussed in terms of svadharma.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “It is better to engage in one’s own occupation, even though one may perform it imperfectly, than to accept another’s occupation and perform it perfectly. Prescribed duties, according to one’s nature, are never affected by sinful reactions.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna says each person does best following the duty that fits his own nature.
hinduism.tie_back: Work should match the person’s nature: the Kural’s வினைக்குரிமை (fitness for a task).
hinduism._accuracy_note: Good on nature-to-duty fit; traditionally tied to the varna system, which Valluvar does not invoke, and the reading of guna as aptitude versus birth is disputed.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Wherefore, brethren, look ye out among you seven men of honest report, full of the Holy Ghost and wisdom, whom we may appoint over this business.”
christianity.explanation: The apostles pick seven qualified men and formally put them in charge of the daily food distribution.
christianity.tie_back: Find the qualified people, then formally give them the task: the Kural’s two steps.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong match: selection by qualification followed by formal appointment.

islam.quote_or_event: “When honesty is lost, then wait for the Hour (Doomsday).” ... “When the power or authority comes in the hands of unfit persons, then wait for the Hour (Doomsday.)”
islam.explanation: The Prophet counts giving authority to unfit people as a sign that honesty has been lost from the world.
islam.tie_back: Authority belongs to those truly suited to it; the hadith states negatively what the Kural states positively.
islam._accuracy_note: Strong inverse match on matching authority to fitness.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Forasmuch as God hath shown thee all this, there is none so discreet and wise as thou. Thou shalt be over my house, and according unto thy word shall all my people be ruled...”
judaism.explanation: Having seen Joseph’s wisdom for himself, Pharaoh gives him full authority over Egypt.
judaism.tie_back: After seeing fitness, Pharaoh makes Joseph the real holder of the office, exactly the Kural’s அதற்குரியனாகச் செயல்.
judaism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one: discern fitness, then confer full authority.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha publicly named particular disciples as foremost (etadagga) in particular qualities: Sariputta in wisdom, Moggallana in psychic power, Upali in monastic discipline, and so on.
buddhism.explanation: He recognised each disciple’s special strength and gave each a matching role and standing.
buddhism.tie_back: Finding each person’s aptitude and giving them standing in it reflects the Kural.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Good on recognising aptitude; the list is honorific rather than a set of work assignments.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Protagoras’ myth, Epimetheus hands out abilities to the animals so that each kind has what suits its way of life, giving speed to some, strength to others, and wings or burrows to others.
greek_mythology.explanation: The myth pictures a world in which capacities are matched to roles.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It dramatises the fit between being and function that the Kural asks rulers to honour.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Loose analogy: matching endowment to function, not appointing workers.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “...one man should practise one thing only, the thing to which his nature was best adapted;—now justice is this principle or a part of it.”
philosophy.explanation: Plato defines justice in the city as each person doing the one task his nature fits him for.
philosophy.tie_back: Plato raises the Kural’s principle, find each person’s fit and make that their work, to the definition of justice.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one on the specialisation principle.

kurals.tamil:
வினைக்கண் வினையுடையான் கேண்மைவே றாக
நினைப்பானை நீங்கும் திரு.
kurals.transliteration:
Vinaikkan vinaiyudaiyaan kenmaive raaga
Ninaippaanai neengum thiru.
kurals.meaning: Fortune abandons the ruler who misreads, and grows suspicious of, the closeness of a man who is devoted to the work entrusted to him.
kurals.elementary: Imagine a kid who works really hard on a group project and is friendly with the teacher, and the teacher starts thinking “he must be up to something.” If you treat your best helpers that way, you lose them, and everything goes wrong.
kurals.university: The couplet warns against a failure of trust after appointment. வினைக்கண் வினையுடையான் is the man wholly absorbed in his assigned work; கேண்மை வேறாக நினைத்தல் is to read his familiarity or friendship with the ruler as something else, such as presumption or disloyalty. Pope renders it as failing to bear the informal friendly ways of such servants, and Pappaiah adds the courtly setting of slanderers who poison the ruler’s mind against capable officers. The penalty is that திரு (prosperity, the goddess of fortune) departs, because a ruler who drives away his best workers destroys his own wealth. Saul’s jealousy of David is the classic Hebrew example.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Mahabharata, Dhritarashtra repeatedly suspects and rebukes his loyal half-brother and minister Vidura, at one point driving him from court, while listening to Duryodhana and his allies; the kingdom ends in ruin.
hinduism.explanation: A king who distrusts his most faithful counsellor loses everything.
hinduism.tie_back: Suspecting the devoted servant drives away fortune, as the Kural warns.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Sabha and Udyoga Parvas (Ganguli trans.)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Good narrative parallel; Vidura is an adviser rather than an executor of tasks.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Who then is a faithful and wise servant, whom his lord hath made ruler over his household, to give them meat in due season? Blessed is that servant, whom his lord when he cometh shall find so doing. Verily I say unto you, That he shall make him ruler over all his goods.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus says a wise master rewards the servant he finds faithfully at work by giving him even more.
christianity.tie_back: The positive side of the Kural: honour the devoted worker, don’t suspect him.
christianity._accuracy_note: The inverse of the Kural (reward rather than the penalty for suspicion); no direct warning against distrust.

islam.quote_or_event: “O you who have believed, if there comes to you a disobedient one with information, investigate, lest you harm a people out of ignorance and become, over what you have done, regretful.”
islam.explanation: Believers are told to check reports from unreliable people before acting, or they may harm the innocent and regret it.
islam.tie_back: This matches Pappaiah’s reading: a ruler must not turn on a loyal worker because of slanderers.
islam._accuracy_note: Strong on the slander dimension; not specific to rulers and workers.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And David had great success in all his ways; and the LORD was with him. And when Saul saw that he had great success, he stood in awe of him.”
judaism.explanation: King Saul grows fearful and suspicious of David, his most successful servant, and tries to kill him; the kingdom passes from Saul’s house.
judaism.tie_back: A ruler who turns on his devoted, effective servant loses his fortune, the Kural’s exact scenario.

buddhism.quote_or_event: According to the Dhammapada commentary, King Pasenadi of Kosala, swayed by jealous courtiers’ slander, had his loyal commander Bandhula and his sons killed; he later learned Bandhula was innocent, and in the end lost his throne with the help of Bandhula’s aggrieved nephew.
buddhism.explanation: A king who distrusts his faithful commander on the word of slanderers brings about his own downfall.
buddhism.tie_back: Fortune leaves the ruler who misreads a loyal worker, as Kural 519 says.
buddhism.source: Dhammapada Commentary, story of Vidudabha (Burlingame, Buddhist Legends)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Strong parallel; the source is commentarial legend, not canonical sutta.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Theseus believes Phaedra’s false accusation against his son Hippolytus without looking into it and curses him; Hippolytus dies, and only then does Theseus learn the truth.
greek_mythology.explanation: A ruler who misjudges a loyal, upright member of his household on false report brings ruin on himself.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This mirrors the Kural’s warning against thinking otherwise of the faithful.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Parallel on misplaced suspicion; a family setting, not employment.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle describes how tyrants keep power by cutting down anyone who stands out, distrusting good and able men, and preferring flatterers, and he treats these as marks of the worst kind of rule.
philosophy.explanation: Suspicion of excellent subordinates is a defining vice of tyranny.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural counts the same suspicion among the things that drive fortune away.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Good conceptual match; Aristotle analyses tyranny rather than giving advice to kings.

kurals.tamil:
நாடோறும் நாடுக மன்னன் வினைசெய்வான்
கோடாமை கோடா துலகு.
kurals.transliteration:
Naadorum naaduga mannan vinaiseyvaan
Kodaamai kodaa thulagu.
kurals.meaning: A king should look into the conduct of those doing his work every day, because as long as they do not go crooked, the world does not go crooked either.
kurals.elementary: A good coach checks on the team at every practice, not just once at the start of the season. If the players stay on track, the whole team does well.
kurals.university: The chapter closes by joining selection to supervision: நாடோறும் நாடுக, examine every day. The logic is causal: if the worker does not swerve (கோடாமை), the world, meaning the realm and its people, will not swerve (கோடாது). Most commentators read it as vigilance over officials, but Kalaignar reads கோடாமை as the worker’s heart not withering, so the king’s daily attention becomes care for the welfare of labour. Kautilya prescribes almost the same thing, that superintendents be examined daily because men are changeable, which gives the Kural a precise parallel in Indian statecraft.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “While engaged in work, they shall be daily examined; for men are naturally fickle-minded, and, like horses at work, exhibit constant change in their temper.”
hinduism.explanation: Kautilya says officials must be checked every day because people’s dispositions shift while they work.
hinduism.tie_back: This is Kural 520’s நாடோறும் நாடுக almost word for word.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Near-verbatim conceptual match in the same genre.

christianity.quote_or_event: “After a long time the lord of those servants cometh, and reckoneth with them.”
christianity.explanation: In the parable of the talents, the master comes back and asks each servant to account for what he did.
christianity.tie_back: Delegation is followed by accountability, though here after a long time rather than every day.
christianity._accuracy_note: Matches accountability; the Kural wants daily oversight, not a single reckoning.

islam.quote_or_event: “All of you are guardians and responsible for your wards and the things under your care. The Imam (i.e. ruler) is the guardian of his subjects and is responsible for them...”
islam.explanation: The Prophet teaches that every ruler answers for those in his care.
islam.tie_back: The ruler’s responsibility for his people requires the constant attention to his agents that the Kural prescribes.
islam._accuracy_note: Strong on the ruler’s responsibility; does not mention daily inspection.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Be thou diligent to know the state of thy flocks, And look well to thy herds;”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs tells the owner to keep close, personal watch over everything in his care.
judaism.tie_back: Diligently knowing the state of your charge is the Kural’s daily examination.
judaism._accuracy_note: Good match on continuing oversight; about flocks rather than officials.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “In five ways should a master minister to his servants and employees as the Nadir : (i) by assigning them work according to their ability, (ii) by supplying them with food and with wages, (iii) by tending them in sickness, (iv) by sharing with them any delicacies, (v) by granting them leave at times.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha tells employers to assign work by ability and look after their workers’ welfare; in return the workers do their duties well.
buddhism.tie_back: This fits the whole chapter’s theme of assigning work by ability, and Kalaignar’s welfare reading of Kural 520.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Excellent on matching work to ability and caring for workers; no explicit daily inspection.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Hesiod says Zeus has countless unseen spirits roaming the earth, watching over human judgments and wrongdoing.
greek_mythology.explanation: In Greek belief, divine oversight keeps an eye on how people act.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Constant watchfulness over those who act on authority parallels the Kural’s daily review of the king’s agents.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Loose analogy: divine surveillance of justice, not a ruler supervising staff.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Xenophon’s Oeconomicus, Ischomachus tells the story of the Persian king who asked what fattens a horse fastest and was told “the master’s eye,” and says the master’s own attention is what makes stewards and estates flourish.
philosophy.explanation: The owner’s personal, continuing oversight is what keeps workers diligent.
philosophy.tie_back: The master’s eye is the Kural’s daily examination.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Strong match on the owner’s continual supervision.
